full_judgment: 6. Mr Ahmed argued that according to the plaintiffs own case, the defendant No. 1 is a co-sharer in exclusive possession and the property is situated in urban area and, as such, he cannot be restrained by an order of status quo. He further submitted that defendant No. 2, a land developer, and defendant No. 1 entered into an agreement to raise multistoried buildings on the land. Defendant No. 2 has already invested huge amount of money (about Taka 1 (one) crore) for laying foundation of the buildings, etc. Therefore, the balance of convenience and inconvenience is in favour of defendants. He further submitted that the plaintiffs in the plaint stated that on 3-2-2003 they came to know from defendant Nos. 1 and 2 that defendant No. 1 got the share of Sabdar Ali by a registered deed of gift on 26-3-1971 and entered into an agreement with defendant No. 2, a land developing company, for construction of multi-storied buildings but they did not bring the suit within reasonable time nor did they make any prayer for injunction or status quo within reasonable time. So, they are not entitled to get an order of injunction/status quo as delay defeats equity. He lastly, submitted that the deed of gift dated 26-3-1971 executed by Sabdar Ali is a registered instrument and, as such, it carries a normal presumption of genuineness till the deed, as alleged by the plaintiffs, is found by the Court to be forged when evidence would be adduced by both the parties. Therefore, for the present, possession of the defendant, on the basis of deed of gift, should not be disturbed. He also cited the case of Fahim-al-Haque (minor) and another vs Mohammad Abdul Aziz and others reported in 43 DLR 226 and submitted that in that case it was held that in the urban areas a co-sharer should not be deprived of using the land in his possession, by making constructions at his own risk. He also cited the case of Nasir Uddin Howlader (Md) vs Abul Kalam, former Chief Engineer of Chittagong Development Authority and others reported in 8 BLC (AD) 156 and submitted that in that case the trial Court allowed the prayer for temporary injunction in a suit for partition in respect of land in urban area and the High Court Division allowed the appeal filed against the order of granting temporary injunction and the Appellate Division refused leave to appeal. It appears that while refusing leave this Division held that in view of the fact that the plaintiff purchased specific 12 decimals of land from RS plot No. 2702 with the boundary and demarcated in a separate holding and he is in actual possession of that 12 decimals of land, the High Court Division committed no illegality in dismissing the appeal. So, it is clear that the facts of the case are distinguishable from the facts of the present case.
